5. As against above submissions, Omar Sadat, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the complainant-respondent banks in Writ petition Nos. 11406 of 2017, 8853 of 2017 and 6109 of 2017 alongwith other learned advocates for other complainant-respondent banks and financial institutions, submits that, all legal formalities as laid down in section 138 of the Act have been duly complied and the materials put forward by the prosecution contain ingredients of criminal offences as contemplated by the section 138 of the Act against the petitioners. There are no legal restrictions upon parties to commence legal proceedings both under section 138 of the Act of 1881 simultaneously with a civil suit, i.e. the Artha Rin suit. They also submit that the cheques were given as "security" at the time of granting loan or any security cheque, do not goes against the scheme of the Act of 1881 and the requirement of depositing signed undated/post dated cheques or otherwise as collateral security against the grant of loan to the petitioners by the Respondent banks does not violate of the provisions of section 5 (P)/5(3) and 7(1) offs ব্যাংক কোম্পানী আইন, ১৯৯১. The petitioners alleged that they gave undated blank cheques as collateral security against the grant of loan to the Respondent banks. The plea taken by the petitioners that the blank cheques have been given by them is of no consequence. There is no law that a person drawing the cheque has to necessarily fill in the same by his own handwriting. Once he has admitted his signature on the cheque, he cannot escape his liability on the ground that the same has not been filled in by him. Actual delivery of cheque or blank cheque is a disputed question of facts and the same cannot be determined by this Court under writ jurisdiction. According to them, if it is the case of the petitioners that the concerned cheques were presented beyond the period of 6 (six) months of the delivery, then they can well put the said case as defense case during trial. In this regard, they have referred to the provisions under section 118 of the NI Act, 1881. According to them, since the statute has given presumption of law in favour of the date mentioned on the cheques, such dates mentioned thereon must be regarded as correct dates until contrary is proved by evidence during trial. They lastly submit that writ petition is not maintainable against the private bank and, as such, these writ petitions are liable to be discharged with costs. 

 22. However, the respondent banks/financial institutions have not presented these cheques for encashment as blank cheques. Admittedly, the cheques were dated and properly filled-up before these were presented to the concerned bank and the petitioners cannot deny the validity of the cheque as per provision of section 120 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which provide that no marker of a promissory note, and no drawer of a bill of exchange or cheque, and no acceptor of a bill of exchange for the honour of the drawer, shall, in a suit thereon by a holder in due course, be permitted to deny the validity of the instrument as originally made or drawn. Further, there is an initial presumption that a negotiable instrument is made, drawn, accepted or endorsed for consideration, but this presumption is a rebuttable presumption, according to the provision of section 118 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The petitioners argued that these cheques subsequently filling-up and the same can only be addressed or put forward by evidence during the trial.
